subtype: Approach: separate accounts for shared bills and personal spending [Action]
passage: Every first of the month, Avni and Abhinav each moved money into their joint account, in proportion to what each earned: Abhinav's share bigger, Avni's smaller. That one account paid the rent, the groceries and the home-loan instalments. Whatever stayed in their own accounts was theirs to spend without explanation. It had begun after an argument about a pair of headphones. Now Abhinav bought comics without a word, and Avni paid for art classes and never had to justify the fees. On a Saturday in Pune, Abhinav came home with a new board game and Avni looked up from the sofa. "Did you check the budget?" "It's my money," said Abhinav, grinning. Avni just smiled. "Have fun." The old friction had gone.

passage:
Manjula looked up from her phone. "Sahil, why is there a cricket bat on our account?"
"Because I bought a cricket bat, Manjula."
"Fourteen hundred rupees?"
"And your three kurtis last week?"
They both stopped. Manjula sat down on the arm of the sofa.
"We keep doing this. Every month we audit each other."
"So what, separate everything?"
"Not everything. One shared account for the rent, groceries and the scooter EMI. You earn more, so you put in more: the same share of each salary. Whatever's left in our own accounts, we spend how we like. No questions."
"No questions even if I buy another bat?"
"Even if you buy ten bats. As long as the shared account is full on the 1st."
"Deal. And I will never mention the kurtis again."
"Good." She smiled. "They were on sale, anyway."

qa.q: How much did the cricket bat cost?
What was Manjula feeling when she sat down on the arm of the sofa?
qa.a: She was tired and a little ashamed of the constant checking, seeing that they audited each other every month.

qa.q: What else could keep the shared account working?
qa.a: They could look at the shared bills together every few months and adjust each person's share if either salary changes.

qa.q: How does Sahil see the new arrangement?
qa.a: Sahil is relieved not to be questioned about personal purchases, and happily promises never to mention the kurtis again.

grounding: It shows a couple agreeing on a shared account for rent, groceries and an EMI funded by the same share of each salary, with the rest spent freely so small arguments fade.

subtype: Approach: separate accounts for shared bills and personal spending [Action]
passage:
For the first year of marriage, Gurpreet and I ran everything from one account, and we argued about it almost every week. Not about rent; about small things. His protein bars. My plants. Every month-end became a trial.
After one particularly silly fight over a four-hundred-rupee fern, we sat down and changed the system. We opened a joint account only for the shared bills: rent, groceries, electricity and the car loan EMI. Gurpreet earns more, so we each put in the same percentage of our salaries on payday, which makes his share bigger. Whatever stays in our own accounts is ours, and nobody asks.
It's been eight months. The joint account has never run short. I bought three more ferns. Gurpreet bought a guitar he hardly plays. Neither of us has said a word. I think that silence is the best part.
— Sarita

qa.q: What was the silly fight about?
What does Sarita mean by "that silence is the best part"?
qa.a: Sarita feels relieved and at peace that small personal choices no longer lead to arguments.

qa.a: They could revisit the percentage each puts into the joint account so the shared bills stay covered fairly.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet experience not being asked about the guitar?
qa.a: Gurpreet likely feels trusted and free to spend his own money without defending it.

grounding: It shows a couple funding a joint account for shared bills in proportion to income and spending the rest freely, which ends their weekly arguments.
